headline: A wildfire destroys 640 buildings in one afternoon

sources.title: Old Trails fire in northwest Spokane destroys 640 structures
The Wildfire Disaster Unfolding In Spokane, Washington
Fires on more than 250,000 acres of Washington state prompt evacuations

chunks.text: A [[wildfire]] {{broke out}} on Saturday, August 1, on open ground west of Spokane, in the eastern half of Washington state. Within hours it had {{torn through}} whole streets on the edge of the city. By Sunday the fire chief for the district said 640 [[structures]] had {{burned down}}, most of them houses, and many of them inside the Spokane city [[limits]]. No deaths have been reported.

verbs.wrong: To burn slowly along the forest floor

verbs.correct: To be destroyed completely by fire
verbs.wrong: To be damaged by heat but still stand

chunks.text: The wind decided the shape of the day. [[Gusts]] {{picked up}} to between 35 and 45 miles an hour and held there for hours, pushing the flames northeast into a state park. From there the fire jumped a river, climbed the [[bluffs]] on the far side and reached the first houses. [[Crews]] could not {{hold back}} a [[front]] moving that fast, and they could not {{put out}} what was already burning, so they worked instead on getting people away from it.

verbs.wrong: To wait for a short time

verbs.correct: To stop a fire from burning
verbs.wrong: To carry water to the fire line

chunks.text: Thousands of people were {{moved out}} of their homes across Spokane County, some with a few minutes' [[notice]]. The city {{set up}} its main [[shelter]] in the [[convention center]] downtown. The mayor declared a city [[emergency]], and the governor declared one for the whole state, {{called in}} the [[National Guard]] and {{brought in}} a [[burn ban]] that covers every county. The cause of the fire is still under [[investigation]].

verbs.correct: To make people leave a place
verbs.wrong: To start living in a new home
To pay the cost of something
To explain a rule to the public

chunks.text: Spokane is not alone. Fires across Washington now {{add up}} to more than 250,000 [[acres]], and smoke has {{built up}} over seven counties badly enough for [[air quality]] warnings. Eastern Washington has spent the summer in record [[drought]], and [[forecasters]] expect dry air and more wind rather than rain. A separate fire north of the city started from a single [[ember]] and took three more houses. What made Saturday different was not that a fire started, but that the wind carried it into a place where people live.
